Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — npm v12 delivers one of the biggest security improvements in years
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm/node install-time spawn downloads Bun runtime (Shai-Hulud worm pattern) · [LLM] Implicit node-gyp rebuild from binding.gyp spawns suspicious build child · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] npm/node install-time process beaconing to webhook.site, sfrclak.com or 142.11.206.73 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] npm install-time process reads .npmrc, SSH key, or cloud-credential file · [LLM] npm lifecycle script harvests secrets via TruffleHog or chains to GitHub API · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
npm/node install-time spawn downloads Bun runtime (Shai-Hulud worm pattern) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud signature where a malicious lifecycle script (preinstall/postinstall) pulls the Bun runtime mid-install to execute the stealer. The article explicitly cites Bun-runtime install during npm setup as a distinguishing behaviour of these worms. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud signature — 'installed the Bun runtime during setup'. Parent-binary set is the canonical npm/yarn/pnpm/node install chain; child predicate binds to the Bun installer URL + binary name. No legitimate package needs Bun mid-npm-install.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer genuinely migrating a project to Bun and adding it as a tooling dep
  • CI image build steps that install Bun in a Dockerfile RUN that also invokes npm in the same layer
  • Internal devx packages that install Bun as part of a polyglot toolchain setup
  • node-based shell wrappers that legitimately `npm exec bun` for repo tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker build","buildkit","buildx") and ProcessCommandLine has "bun.sh/install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree from DeviceProcessEvents around the alert — confirm `npm install` / `npm ci` was the originating command and identify the specific package whose lifecycle script kicked it off (usually visible in InitiatingProcessParentCommandLine or the working-directory node_modules path). 2) Contain: isolate the device, revoke any npm publish tokens, GitHub PATs, and SSH keys that lived on it (Shai-Hulud worms exfil all three), kill the dev's session, and pin the package version in the lockfile registry-wide. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId for outbound to webhook.site / sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73 and trufflehog/secret-scanner spawns within the next 10 minutes; check GitHub audit log for new public repos created by the user's PAT in the last 24h.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let InstallParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","node.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","corepack.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (InstallParents)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","preinstall","postinstall")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","github.com/oven-sh/bun","bun install","bun run","\\bun.exe","/bun ")
   or FileName =~ "bun.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let InstallParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","node.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","corepack.exe"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ParentProcessName has_any (InstallParents)
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","preinstall","postinstall")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","github.com/oven-sh/bun","bun install","bun run","\\bun.exe","/bun ")
   or ActingProcessName endswith "bun.exe"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm/node lifecycle script downloads Bun runtime (Shai-Hulud)
id: 4b8f1c2a-7d3e-4d6a-9a1f-1e2c5b9a0d11
description: A package-manager install (npm/yarn/pnpm) or node-driven lifecycle script pulls the Bun runtime mid-install, the signature step of the Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud worms.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent_selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npx.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
  child_selection:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'bun.sh/install'
      - 'github.com/oven-sh/bun'
      - 'bun install'
      - 'bun run'
      - '\bun.exe'
  condition: parent_selection and child_selection
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:(1 OR 4688) @ParentImage:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\npx.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe) @CommandLine:(*bun.sh/install* OR *github.com/oven-sh/bun* OR *"bun install"* OR *"bun run"* OR *\\bun.exe*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(npm|node|npx|yarn|pnpm|corepack)\.exe$/i
| (CommandLine=/bun\.sh\/install/i OR CommandLine=/github\.com\/oven-sh\/bun/i OR CommandLine=/bun\s+install/i OR CommandLine=/bun\s+run/i OR ImageFileName=/\\bun\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_path) as image from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") OR Processes.parent_process IN ("*\\npm install*","*npm ci*","* preinstall *","* postinstall *")) (Processes.process IN ("*bun.exe*","*/bun*","*bun install*","*bun run*","*curl*bun.sh/install*","*iwr*bun.sh*","*Invoke-WebRequest*bun.sh*","*github.com/oven-sh/bun*")) by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_path) as image from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") OR Processes.parent_process IN ("*\\npm install*","*npm ci*","* preinstall *","* postinstall *")) (Processes.process IN ("*bun.exe*","*/bun*","*bun install*","*bun run*","*curl*bun.sh/install*","*iwr*bun.sh*","*Invoke-WebRequest*bun.sh*","*github.com/oven-sh/bun*")) by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
npm/node install-time process beaconing to webhook.site, sfrclak.com or 142.11.206.73 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the exfil-leg of the article's named campaigns where an install-time lifecycle script beacons to webhook.site (canary inbox) or to known campaign infrastructure (sfrclak.com, 142.11.206.73) to ship harvested tokens. High-fidelity because legitimate npm packages do not POST credentials to webhook.site mid-install. Rationale: Hard IOCs from the article: domain sfrclak.com, IP 142.11.206.73, and webhook.site as the canary inbox commonly used by the Shai-Hulud lineage. Binding the egress to an npm/node/yarn/pnpm/bun process gates out personal webhook.site usage by developers in unrelated tooling. Sentinel query unioned across ImDnsActivity / ImNetworkSession / ImProcessCreate — no DeviceName references on tables that don't carry it.
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer testing their own webhook.site inbox via a quick node REPL or `curl`-via-`npm exec` — match on InitiatingProcessParentFileName==cmd/powershell rather than npm-lifecycle parent
  • Legitimate package using webhook.site as a documented test endpoint (rare, vet by package name)
  • An internal reverse-proxy that legitimately resolves to 142.11.206.73 (verify with NetOps before suppressing)
  • Pre-existing Aikido / SafeChain telemetry callbacks if a competitor product uses webhook.site for ack
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("safe-chain","aikido") and RemoteUrl has "webhook.site")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceProcessEvents on the same DeviceId 5 minutes before the network event to identify the originating `npm install` and the specific package directory under node_modules (the script body usually drops in postinstall.js / telemetry.js / index.js of the rogue package). 2) Contain: yank network from the host, revoke npm publish tokens + GitHub PATs + cloud SSO sessions for the developer, block sfrclak.com + 142.11.206.73 at perimeter, and add the package@version to your internal denylist. 3) Hunt: tstats 30 days back for any other host that contacted those same IOCs from a node-family parent; check GitHub for new repos named like `Shai-Hulud-*` or with the user's PAT scoped to public-repo create.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectDomains = dynamic(["webhook.site","sfrclak.com"]);
let SuspectIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
let InstallProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (InstallProcs)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (InstallProcs)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","preinstall","postinstall")
| where RemoteUrl has_any (SuspectDomains)
   or RemoteIP in (SuspectIPs)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectDomains = dynamic(["webhook.site","sfrclak.com"]);
let SuspectIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
let InstallProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
let DnsHits = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where DnsQuery has_any (SuspectDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, SrcHost = SrcHostname, SrcIp = SrcIpAddr,
              Indicator = DnsQuery, Source = "DNS";
let NetHits = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where DstIpAddr in (SuspectIPs) or DstHostname has_any (SuspectDomains) or Url has_any (SuspectDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, SrcHost = SrcHostname, SrcIp = SrcIpAddr,
              Indicator = coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr, Url), Source = "Net";
let ProcHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (InstallProcs) or ParentProcessName has_any (InstallProcs)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspectDomains) or ActingProcessCommandLine has "142.11.206.73"
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, SrcHost = DvcHostname, SrcIp = DvcIpAddr,
              Indicator = ActingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Proc";
union DnsHits, NetHits, ProcHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Implicit node-gyp rebuild from binding.gyp spawns suspicious build child AIInstallation Medium
Targets the new attack surface the article highlights — packages without any declared scripts that still execute code via an implicit `node-gyp rebuild` triggered by binding.gyp. Detects node-gyp invoking compilers / interpreters / network tools that don't belong in a native-module build. Rationale: The article specifically names the binding.gyp / implicit `node-gyp rebuild` path as a covert execution channel that v12 will block. Genuine native-module builds spawn compilers (cl.exe, link.exe, gyp.exe) — they should never need powershell/curl/certutil. Child set is the standard LOLBin/network-downloader allowlist.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Native module that legitimately shells out to powershell to detect Windows SDK / Visual Studio paths (some node-canvas / node-sass forks)
  • node-pre-gyp using curl/wget to fetch prebuilt binaries (legitimate but article-relevant — review)
  • Developer environments running `npm install` with --verbose where parent-cmdline chaining produces false parents
  • CI nodes that wrap node-gyp in a shell script for cross-compilation
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-pre-gyp","prebuild-install") and FileName =~ "curl.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "github.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the package owning the binding.gyp from the working directory in InitiatingProcessFolderPath (look under node_modules/<pkg>/binding.gyp), pull the SHA256 of the child binary, and dump the script body if the child is a scripting host. 2) Contain: quarantine the package version, remove from internal mirror/proxy, kick CI jobs that pulled it in the last 24h, and rotate any developer-tier secrets present in the build environment. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceFileEvents for files written under %TEMP%/%APPDATA%/.npm/_cacache during the build window, and DeviceNetworkEvents for non-prebuilt-binary URLs (anything outside github.com/<pkg> releases or the org's artifact registry).
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let UnexpectedChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "binding.gyp"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "npm install"
      and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp rebuild"
| where FileName in~ (UnexpectedChildren)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let UnexpectedChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","binding.gyp","node-gyp rebuild")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (UnexpectedChildren)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: node-gyp implicit rebuild spawns scripting/networking child
id: 9c1a8d54-2b7e-4c5f-a9d1-04e2f7a8c133
description: A node-gyp build (often triggered implicitly during npm install by a package's binding.gyp) spawns a shell, scripting host, or network downloader — the covert execution path the npm v12 allowlist is designed to close.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent_selection:

      - 'node-gyp'

  child_selection:

      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentCommandLine:(*node-gyp* OR *binding.gyp* OR *"node-gyp rebuild"*) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (regex("node-gyp", field=ParentProcessCommandLine) OR regex("binding\.gyp", field=ParentProcessCommandLine))
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|wscript|cscript|curl|wget|certutil|bitsadmin|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32)\.exe$/i

npm install-time process reads .npmrc, SSH key, or cloud-credential file AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-harvesting step of Nx s1ngularity / Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud — install-time scripts read .npmrc (auth tokens), ~/.ssh/id_* (SSH keys), and AWS/GitHub credential files. The article lists these exact artefacts as what the postinstall payloads scrape. Rationale: Article enumerates exactly these victim artefacts — 'scans for tokens, SSH keys, and other goodies', and Nx s1ngularity is called out specifically as harvesting GitHub tokens, npm credentials, SSH keys, and crypto wallets. Filtering on install-time parent + ≥2 credential-file hits in one process strips out IDE indexing noise while keeping the harvester pattern.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm CLI reading user's own .npmrc during publish/login (filter on npm-cli.js parent + 'npm publish' command line)
  • VS Code remote-ssh extension's node host enumerating ~/.ssh during workspace open
  • yarn classic touching .npmrc to migrate auth tokens on first install
  • Developer running aws-sdk-node example that reads ~/.aws/credentials intentionally
Suppression filter
| where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm whoami") and TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the originating process tree and the package directory under node_modules to identify the rogue package; capture the script body before the file deletes itself (article notes the harvesters self-delete). 2) Contain: immediately rotate every credential the process touched — npm tokens via `npm token revoke`, GitHub PATs in GH settings, AWS keys via IAM, force-push SSH key re-keying. Quarantine the host. 3) Hunt: search GitHub audit logs for new public repos created by the user's PAT in the last 24h (Shai-Hulud uploads stolen creds to public repos), pivot to other hosts that installed the same package@version via your internal registry logs.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let InstallProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
let CredPaths = dynamic([".npmrc",".ssh\\id_rsa",".ssh\\id_ed25519",".ssh\\id_ecdsa",".aws\\credentials",".config\\gh\\hosts.yml",".gitconfig",".netrc","npm\\.npmrc"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType in ("FileOpened","FileRead","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (InstallProcs)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (InstallProcs)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","postinstall","preinstall")
| where FolderPath has_any (CredPaths) or FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize CredFiles = make_set(strcat(FolderPath, "\\", FileName), 25),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hits = count()
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
               InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where Hits >= 2 or array_length(CredFiles) >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let InstallProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
let CredPaths = dynamic([".npmrc",".ssh/id_rsa",".ssh/id_ed25519",".ssh/id_ecdsa",".aws/credentials",".config/gh/hosts.yml",".gitconfig",".netrc"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType in ("FileAccessed","FileCreated","FileModified","FileRead")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (InstallProcs)
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install","postinstall","preinstall")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (CredPaths) or TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize CredFiles = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count()
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where Hits >= 2 or array_length(CredFiles) >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\bun.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc* OR *\\.ssh\\id_rsa* OR *\\.ssh\\id_ed25519* OR *\\.aws\\credentials* OR *\\.config\\gh\\hosts.yml* OR *\\.netrc*)
(#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten) ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|npx|yarn|pnpm|bun)\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\\\\\.npmrc|\\\\\\.ssh\\\\id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\\\\\\.aws\\\\credentials|\\\\\\.config\\\\gh\\\\hosts\\.yml|\\\\\\.netrc)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| count > 1

npm lifecycle script harvests secrets via TruffleHog or chains to GitHub API AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud-specific behaviour the article describes — install-time scripts that download and run TruffleHog to scrape secrets, then chain to a GitHub API call (api.github.com) to publish stolen credentials to a public repo. High-fidelity because TruffleHog under an npm-install parent is otherwise zero. Rationale: Article names both 'ran TruffleHog to scrape secrets' and 'dumped them into public GitHub repos' as the Shai-Hulud signature. Public-repo creation via api.github.com/user/repos or `gh repo create --public` under a node-family parent has no benign workflow we've ever seen.
ATT&CKT1552 T1567.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security-team CI job that legitimately runs TruffleHog as a pre-commit/post-install secret-scan in a sanctioned pipeline — tag those hosts and exclude
  • Developer running `npm exec gh-action-secrets-scan` in a sanctioned tool
  • A package that bundles trufflehog as a transitive dependency for its OWN secret-scanning feature (rare; vet by package name)
  • Internal devx tool that auto-creates public template repos on first install
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sec-ci","appsec-runner") and ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the originating npm-install command and rogue package version from process-tree context, snapshot the working directory before self-deletion, and record the SHA256 of any trufflehog.exe / gitleaks.exe binary dropped. 2) Contain: revoke all developer secrets in scope (GitHub PAT, npm tokens, SSH, AWS, cloud SSO), force-delete any public repo created by the user's PAT in the last 24h via `gh repo delete --yes`, quarantine the host, denylist the package version. 3) Hunt: query GitHub audit logs for `repo.create` + `repo.public` events by the user in 48h window, search EmailEvents for any maintainer-targeted phishing in the prior week (article notes the worm starts with a maintainer phish), and pivot to other internal hosts that pulled the package via internal-registry access logs.
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let InstallParents = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
let ScraperIndicators = dynamic(["trufflehog","gitleaks","detect-secrets","api.github.com/user/repos","gh repo create --public","Shai-Hulud"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (InstallParents)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (InstallParents)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","npm install","npm ci")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (ScraperIndicators)
   or FileName has_any ("trufflehog.exe","gitleaks.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let InstallParents = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe"]);
let ScraperIndicators = dynamic(["trufflehog","gitleaks","detect-secrets","api.github.com/user/repos","gh repo create --public","Shai-Hulud"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ParentProcessName has_any (InstallParents)
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","npm install","npm ci")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (ScraperIndicators)
   or ActingProcessName has_any ("trufflehog.exe","gitleaks.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.11.206.73") or RemoteUrl has_any ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["sfrclak.com", "webhook.site"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("142.11.206.73")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("142.11.206.73")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

Unauthenticated HTTP POST to Meta Ads MCP /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 (CVE-2026-48039) AIDelivery Medium
Detects external/unauthenticated callers reaching the vulnerable Meta Ads MCP Streamable HTTP endpoint. Hunts inbound POSTs to /mcp on TCP 8080 from public sources, which the AuthInjectionMiddleware fails to challenge with 401 and forwards directly to tool handlers. Rationale: Targets the article's exact exploitation primitive — unauthenticated POST to /mcp on default port 8080 receiving HTTP 200 (per PoC step 1). Filtering out RFC1918 / loopback eliminates internal app-server health checks and keeps focus on attacker-reachable exposure. Port + path + method + public source is high-fidelity for CVE-2026-48039.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate external integrations / partner CRMs invoking the MCP endpoint with proper auth headers (refine with auth-header check at WAF)
  • Internet-exposed dev/staging environments deliberately left without auth for testing
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7) probing /mcp from known scanner CIDRs
  • CDN/WAF health probes reaching the origin with synthetic POST traffic
  • Penetration test traffic during sanctioned engagements
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("--healthcheck", "readiness", "liveness") and RemoteIP !in (dynamic(["<trusted_partner_ip_1>","<scanner_cidr>"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the source IP is external and unexpected — check WAF logs for the same SourceIP making prior /mcp calls; review request body for `tools/call` method names like `get_ad_accounts`. Pull the matching HTTP response and grep for `access_token=` in the JSON body — if present, the Meta token has already leaked. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP at the WAF/edge immediately. Take the MCP service offline or front it with an auth-enforcing reverse proxy (return 401 on missing Authorization). Rotate the `META_ACCESS_TOKEN` environment variable on the host and revoke any long-lived Meta Graph API tokens issued to that operator account from the Meta Business Manager. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC #2 — search outbound network logs from this host to `graph.facebook.com` with `access_token=` in the URL. Audit Meta ad-account activity for unauthorized ad creation, budget changes, or read operations from unknown IPs in the past 30 days. Identify all other hosts running `meta-ads

| where RemoteIPType == "Public"

Meta Graph API access_token leak in outbound URL query (CVE-2026-48039 exfiltration) AICommand & Control High
Detects the specific token-leak pathway from api.py:136 — outbound HTTPS to graph.facebook.com carrying access_token= in the URL query string. Catches both the vulnerable server's outbound call AND attacker-side reuse of the stolen token from any host. Rationale: References the exact strings from api.py:136 (`request_params["access_token"] = access_token` then appended to URL) and the article's PoC trace showing `graph.facebook.com/v24.0/me/adaccounts?...&access_token=FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789`. The combination `graph.facebook.com` + `access_token=` in URL is the high-fidelity leakage signature — Meta's official SDKs use Authorization header, so URL-query token usage is anomalous. Detects both the vulnerable server's pre-error outbound and downstream attacker reuse.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy in-house Meta Ads integrations that still pass access_token in the URL instead of Authorization header
  • Marketing-team CLI tools or one-off curl debugging sessions against Graph API
  • Third-party analytics SaaS connectors with older Meta SDK versions
  • Pre-CVE-fix internal traffic from sanctioned meta-ads-mcp instances on patched versions still using the old token format
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("--legacy-auth", "meta-sdk-v1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the URL substring with access_token preview and identify the originating host + process. If host is a meta-ads-mcp server, treat as confirmed CVE-2026-48039 exfiltration; if host is unrelated, suspect attacker reuse of a leaked token. Step 2 (contain): Immediately revoke the leaked Meta access token via Meta Business Manager > Business Settings > System Users > Access Tokens. Rotate `META_ACCESS_TOKEN` env var on all meta-ads-mcp hosts. Block outbound to graph.facebook.com from the source host pending investigation if it's not an expected ad-tooling server. Step 3 (hunt): Query Meta Business Manager / Meta Ads Manager activity log for the affected ad account: look for unauthorized ad creations, budget changes, ad-account user adds, or read operations from unfamiliar IPs in the past 30 days. Search 90 days of proxy logs for the same token-preview substring to map every host that touched the token. Correlate with UC #1 hits to identify the originating exploitatio

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "graph.facebook.com"
| where RemoteUrl has "access_token="
| extend TokenPreview = extract(@"access_token=([A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{6,12})", 1, RemoteUrl)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, TokenPreview,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

(ImWebSession

Vulnerable meta-ads-mcp installation inventory (CVE-2026-48039) AIReconnaissance High
Asset-management hunt for hosts running pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp at vulnerable versions (<= 1.0.101 confirmed, 1.0.102-1.0.108 unconfirmed). Combines TVM inventory with live-process detection for Docker / uvicorn / gunicorn launching the package. Rationale: References the article's exact package name (pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp), the import path (meta_ads_mcp/core/), and vulnerable version range. Process-based discovery catches Docker-deployed instances where TVM may not enumerate the pip package; TVM lookup catches host-installed pip versions. Combining both gives full coverage.
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1518.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched versions (≥ 1.0.109) still match by package name — version filtering in downstream triage required
  • Development laptops running meta-ads-mcp locally for testing (not internet-exposed but still inventory-relevant)
  • CI/CD runners temporarily executing meta-ads-mcp during package builds
  • Forks/clones of the package under different folder paths
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each host returned, capture installed version. If <= 1.0.101 confirm vulnerable; if 1.0.102-1.0.108 escalate to package owner since patch status is unconfirmed per the advisory. Check whether port 8080 is internet-exposed using DeviceNetworkInfo + perimeter scan results. Step 2 (contain): For internet-exposed vulnerable hosts: front the MCP service with an auth-enforcing reverse proxy or restrict to internal CIDR via firewall; rotate any `META_ACCESS_TOKEN` env vars. For internal-only vulnerable hosts: schedule a patch within the standard SLA window. Step 3 (hunt): Run UC #1 and UC #2 against the discovered hosts for the past 30 days to determine if any of them have already been exploited. Pivot to package-manager logs (`pip install meta-ads-mcp`) to identify how the vulnerable version spread.

Meta Ads MCP PoC artefact creation or execution (poc.py / http_auth_integration.py exploit staging) AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts for the appearance of the article's named PoC and exploit files on managed hosts. Targets `poc.py` (attacker tool) on any host plus modifications to `http_auth_integration.py` / `api.py` under a `meta_ads_mcp/core` folder path — useful for catching either exploit staging or unauthorised patches. Rationale: References the article's exact PoC filename (`poc.py`) and the two vulnerable source files cited by line number (`http_auth_integration.py:272`, `api.py:136`). The folder-path qualifier `meta_ads_mcp/core` filters out the ~10000 other api.py files that exist in any Python ecosystem. Catches three scenarios: PoC tool dropped on victim, attacker-modified core files post-compromise, or sanctioned patches an analyst should know about.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers cloning pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp for local testing
  • Security team deploying CVE patches to http_auth_integration.py / api.py
  • Generic poc.py files unrelated to this CVE (security research projects, CTF artefacts, training material)
  • Automated package re-installs via pip/poetry that recreate the core files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in (dynamic(["<approved_devs>","<patching_svc_acct>"])) and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any (dynamic(["\\ide\\","\\pycharm\\","\\vscode\\"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For poc.py hits, capture the file SHA256 and compare to known IOCs; check the parent process (was it a developer's IDE or an unexpected service?). For http_auth_integration.py / api.py modifications, diff the file against the upstream 1.0.109+ patched version to determine if it's a legitimate patch or attacker tampering. Step 2 (contain): If poc.py was executed against a meta-ads-mcp host: revoke META_ACCESS_TOKEN immediately, kill the meta-ads-mcp process, and isolate the host pending forensics. If unauthorised core file modification: snapshot the host and revert to known-good package version. Step 3 (hunt): From the InitiatingProcessAccountName, pivot to UserLogon events on that account in the past 30 days — look for unusual source IPs or off-hours access. Search shell history (.bash_history, PowerShell ScriptBlock logs) for related commands like `curl http://*/mcp` or `docker run *meta-ads-mcp*`. Cross-reference with UC #1 hits from the same source IP.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Cybersecurity Stars Awards 2026: Winners Announced Across 95 Categories
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the three hard-coded GitHub commit-search query strings the Miasma supply-chain worm uses as its three independent C2 channels (PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, Python payload delivery). These strings have zero legitimate business presence and are the highest-fidelity Miasma indicator available. Rationale: The three strings 'DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom', 'TheBeautifulSandsOfTime' and 'firedalazer' are the hard-coded GitHub commit-search queries each Miasma C2 channel uses (PAT discovery, JS payload, Python payload). They are confirmed by SafeDep's analysis, BleepingComputer's report, and a parallel TheHackerNews write-up. Zero legitimate business processes contain these tokens. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-supply-chain-attack-compromises.html • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst running these strings through their own grep/search tooling for hunting
  • SOC engineer pasting the IOCs into a script or note file
  • Security researcher cloning or reading SafeDep / Cloudsmith write-ups in a developer IDE that logs URL paths
  • Sandbox / detonation environment intentionally executing a Miasma sample for analysis
  • Automation that ingests OSS-supply-chain advisories and writes IOCs to a database column
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe") and not (FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\","\\detonation\\","\\analyst-tools\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process that emitted the string is not an analyst hunting tool, a CTI ingestion script, or a known sandbox. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain; if the string was in a network URL, identify what process issued the GET against api.github.com/search/commits. 2) Contain: if the originating process is a node/python/git/curl invocation on a developer machine or CI runner, isolate the host from network, revoke any GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems publish tokens and JFrog Artifactory credentials owned by that user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same three strings org-wide; pivot on the parent process and SHA256 to find sibling executions; review the developer's git push history for npm/PyPI/RubyGems package versions published in the last 7d for unexpected new releases or postinstall scripts.
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256, Source = strcat("Net:", RemoteUrl);
union ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
union From4688, FromAsim
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts for git clone / npm install / pip install / curl / wget operations that reference the briefly-public 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' GitHub repositories which leaked the worm's source on 2026-06-08. A match means the host has either ingested the leaked toolkit or is being staged with it. Rationale: 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' is the exact repository slug SafeDep and BleepingComputer report appeared on GitHub from 2026-06-08 hosting the leaked toolkit. The string is uniquely tied to Miasma and would only surface in dev-tool command lines or proxy URLs when a host is cloning, installing or downloading the leaked source. Cross-checked via SafeDep, BleepingComputer and TheRegister. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1105 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel team intentionally cloning the leaked repo into a sandbox for analysis
  • Security researcher fetching the source on a developer workstation for write-up
  • SOAR / TIP ingesting OSS advisory feeds and storing the repo URL as an IOC string
  • Vulnerability scanner or SCA tool fingerprinting against known-malicious repo names
  • Blue-team CTF or training environment seeding the toolkit deliberately
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\") and FolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process that issued the clone/install/fetch — confirm it is not a sanctioned analyst sandbox or CTI ingestion job. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and any subsequent npm/pip postinstall script execution from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node/python child processes spawned within 1 hour of the clone, revoke GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems/Artifactory publish tokens belonging to the user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the three Miasma C2 commit-search strings (see related UC) on the same host and across the org; review the user's recent package publishes for unexpected versions; check GitHub Actions workflows in any repo they touched for newly-added steps referencing untrusted secrets or external scripts.
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let DevTools = dynamic(["git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (DevTools) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevTools)
    | where ProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Network";
union isfuzzy=true ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or TargetProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
let FromProxy = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL contains MiasmaRepo or DestinationHostName contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, Account = SourceUserName, NewProcessName = "", CommandLine = RequestURL, ParentProcessName = "", Source = "Proxy";
union From4688, FromAsim, FromProxy
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores

description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 10 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

For thirty years, vulnerability management ran on a buffer: the months between when a vulnerability was found and when someone could figure out how to weaponize it. The solution was straightforward enough; triage by severity, schedule the fix, validate, and move on. The buffer was what made that work. Today, that buffer is gone. AI didn't make your team slower. It changed the other side of the
